meta.title: Terrestrial Ledger — annual land CO2 uptake by region

sources.gcb: Friedlingstein et al. 2025, Global Carbon Budget 2025, Earth Syst. Sci. Data 18, 3211-3288, doi:10.5194/essd-18-3211-2026; data doi:10.18160/GCP-2025 (spreadsheet via ICOS Carbon Portal)
sources.regions: Friedlingstein et al. 2025, Sect. 3.8.2 and Figure 15: decadal-mean (2015-2024) land fluxes for the 10 RECCAP-2 land regions
sources.gcos: GCOS Essential Climate Variables, terrestrial domain (20 ECVs), gcos.wmo.int/en/essential-climate-variables (accessed 2026-11-26); framework GTOS/TOPC, sponsored jointly by GCOS, the FAO-led GTOS and WCRP
sources.processes: Beer et al. 2010; Bond-Lamberty & Thomson 2010; Batjes 1996; Jobbagy & Jackson 2000; Hugelius et al. 2014; van der Werf et al. 2017 (GFED4.1s)

notes: GCB land sink (SLAND) is the natural land uptake: the average of 22 dynamic global vegetation models (S2 simulation), RSS-adjusted for land-cover bias, uncertainty +-0.5 GtC/yr on average (wider in single years; +-1.1 GtC/yr in 2024).

Regional fluxes are DECADAL MEANS (2015-2024) from GCB 2025 Fig. 15 / Sect. 3.8.2, not an annual series. No published annual regional land series exists. Values stated in the paper text are exact; the rest are read from Figure 15 to the nearest 0.05 GtC/yr (value_source 'fig'). Net flux = SLAND - ELUC; positive = sink.

Regional DGVM nets sum to more than the global net land flux (SLAND minus bookkeeping ELUC) because DGVMs underestimate ELUC in South America and Southeast Asia (GCB 2025 Sect. 3.8.2). The page states the reconciliation.
Sign convention on this page: uptake is positive (carbon into the land); ELUC is shown as a positive emission (carbon out of the land).

summary.preliminary_2025_source: Ciais et al. 2026, low-latency global carbon budget 2025, arXiv:2609.34226 (2.36 +- 0.16 GtC/yr; preliminary, not in the GCB series). NOTE: this is the NET land flux (sink minus land-use emissions), a different quantity from the SLAND series plotted here.

North America.drivers: Boreal and temperate forests, regrowing after past clearing and fertilised by rising CO₂, give a steady sink, and net land-use losses are near zero. The sink is now being cut by fire: Canada's record 2023 fires and three straight high years — January–September 2025 fire emissions of 0.3–0.4 GtC, 2.2× the 2015–2024 average.
ecvs: Fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR)

South America.drivers: The Amazon is the largest tropical forest carbon store, but deforestation and degradation emit about 0.5 GtC/yr (bookkeeping), nearly cancelling the natural sink. Inversions see a small net source; DGVMs a small sink — the disagreement is the budget's largest regional uncertainty. The 2023–24 El Niño drought turned tropical lands into a source.
ecvs: Fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR)

Europe.drivers: Managed forests and farmland regrowth give a modest sink; inversions (0.3 GtC/yr) see more than DGVMs (0.1). Land-use emissions are near zero.
ecvs: Fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR)

Africa.drivers: Congo Basin forest and savannahs fix about 0.5 GtC/yr, but deforestation, shifting cultivation and fire emit about 0.4 GtC/yr — Africa contributes about half of global fire emissions. Inversions see a net source (−0.3); DGVMs a small sink (0.1).
ecvs: Fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR)

Russia.drivers: Boreal forest and tundra: the largest inversion sink (0.6 GtC/yr) but DGVMs say 0.3 — the paper's north–south conundrum in one region. Permafrost holds ~1,300 PgC beneath it; thaw is the long-term risk.

West Asia.drivers: Arid and semi-arid lands: small fluxes, near-neutral. Water, not carbon, is the limiting factor — irrigation and groundwater set what grows.

Southeast Asia.drivers: Peat swamp forests store huge carbon per hectare; draining and burning them emits 0.4 GtC/yr (bookkeeping) — twice what DGVMs simulate, which the paper flags as a likely DGVM underestimate. Net: about neutral by DGVMs, a source by inversions.
ecvs: Fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR)

East Asia.drivers: Regrowing forests — above all China's afforestation — plus intensive cropland give a 0.2 GtC/yr sink that both methods agree on. Land-use emissions are near zero.
ecvs: Fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR)

South Asia.drivers: Monsoon-fed croplands and forests: a small sink (about 0.0–0.2 GtC/yr), strongly tied to monsoon rain and irrigation.

Australasia.drivers: Arid interior and savannahs: a small, wildly variable sink — wet years store carbon, drought and fire years release it. ENSO sets the rhythm.

ecvs.name: Groundwater
ecvs.role: Water stored below ground sustains dry-season growth and sets drought resilience.

ecvs.name: Lakes
ecvs.role: Lake area and level track water storage; lakes bury carbon in sediments.

ecvs.name: River discharge
ecvs.role: Rivers carry land carbon to the sea — the GCB's river-outgassing adjustment is 0.65 GtC/yr.

ecvs.name: Terrestrial water storage
ecvs.role: GRACE-measured water storage; land-flux anomalies track it (Ciais et al. 2026).

ecvs.name: Evaporation from land
ecvs.role: The water flux that accompanies photosynthesis; drought cuts both together.

ecvs.name: Soil moisture
ecvs.role: Controls photosynthesis, respiration and fire risk — the master switch on the sink's year-to-year swings.

ecvs.name: Glaciers
ecvs.role: Meltwater and newly exposed land; a small direct carbon role, a large climate signal.

ecvs.name: Ice sheets and ice shelves
ecvs.role: Not a carbon flux itself; their melt sets sea level and the long-term climate the sink lives in.

ecvs.name: Permafrost
ecvs.role: Thaw releases the ~1,300 PgC stored in permafrost-region soils as CO₂ and CH₄.

ecvs.name: Snow
ecvs.role: Insulates soil, sets the spring thaw and the start of the growing season.

ecvs.name: Above-ground biomass
ecvs.role: The living carbon stock (~550 GtC in vegetation); its change is the sink.

ecvs.name: Albedo
ecvs.role: How much sunlight land reflects; darkening warms and brightening cools — a feedback on the sink.

ecvs.name: Fire
ecvs.role: Satellite fire counts and burned area give fire emissions, about 2 GtC/yr.

ecvs.name: Fraction of absorbed photosynthetically active radiation (FAPAR)
ecvs.role: The fraction of sunlight plants absorb — the direct satellite measure of photosynthesis at work.

ecvs.name: Land cover
ecvs.role: What grows where; deforestation and regrowth show up here first.

ecvs.name: Land surface temperature
ecvs.role: Heat stress cuts photosynthesis and raises respiration.

ecvs.name: Leaf area index
ecvs.role: Leaf area per ground area; sets how much light the canopy can catch.

ecvs.name: Soil carbon
ecvs.role: The stock itself (~1,500 GtC in the top metre) and its change.

ecvs.name: Anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions
ecvs.role: Fossil + land-use emissions — the denominator the sink is measured against.

ecvs.name: Anthropogenic water use
ecvs.role: Irrigation and extraction change soil moisture, growth and river flow.

processes.name: Photosynthesis — gross primary production
processes.role: Plants fix about 123 ± 8 PgC/yr from the air (Beer et al. 2010) — the largest carbon flux on Earth, roughly ten times fossil-fuel emissions. Tropical forests and savannahs do 60% of it. Every tonne in the land sink entered through this door.

processes.name: Plant & soil respiration
processes.role: Nearly all of GPP returns to the air as CO₂. Soils alone breathe out 98 ± 12 PgC/yr (Bond-Lamberty & Thomson 2010), rising about 0.1 PgC/yr as the planet warms, with a temperature sensitivity (Q10) of about 1.5. The sink is what photosynthesis keeps ahead of respiration.

processes.name: Soil carbon storage
processes.role: Soils hold about 1,500 GtC of organic carbon in the top metre (Batjes 1996; Jobbágy & Jackson 2000) — roughly twice the carbon in the air and three times the ~550 GtC in vegetation. Litter feeds it, microbes eat it; the balance is the slow store.

processes.name: Permafrost carbon
processes.role: Permafrost-region soils hold about 1,300 PgC (range 1,100–1,500), some 800 PgC of it perennially frozen (Hugelius et al. 2014). Thaw releases it as CO₂ and CH₄ — about 18 GtC per degree of global warming (IPCC 2021). The DGVMs behind the land sink mostly do not simulate abrupt thaw.

processes.name: Fire disturbance
processes.role: Fire returns about 2 GtC/yr to the air in a typical recent year (GFED4.1s). 2023–2024 ran hot — 1.7–2.2 GtC in January–September alone, driven by Canada's record fires — while Africa contributes about half of global fire emissions (GCB 2025 §3.8.3).
processes.source: van der Werf et al. 2017 (GFED4.1s); GCB 2025 §3.8.3

processes.name: Land-use change
processes.role: Clearing forest and draining peat emits 1.25 GtC/yr (2024, GCB 2025), and regrowth on abandoned land takes some back. It is the only process humans directly control, and the largest uncertainty in the budget (±0.7 GtC/yr).

processes.name: The small difference of huge fluxes
processes.role: GPP (~123 PgC/yr) minus respiration and fire leaves a net sink of about 2 GtC/yr — roughly 2% of what photosynthesis fixes. That is why the land sink swings by ±1 GtC from year to year with drought and El Niño, why its uncertainty (±0.5–1.1 GtC/yr) is large next to its size, and why climate change — which cut the 2015–2024 sink by 25% (GCB 2025) — matters so much. Warming raises respiration (Q10 ≈ 1.5) and fire, while rising CO₂ fertilises photosynthesis; the balance is what the annual series measures.

region_reconciliation.note: The ten regional DGVM net fluxes sum to 1.3 GtC/yr, above the global 2015-2024 mean net land flux (SLAND minus bookkeeping ELUC) of 0.99 GtC/yr. The gap is the DGVM underestimate of ELUC: in South America the bookkeeping models put ELUC at ~0.5 GtC/yr against ~0.3 in the DGVMs, and in Southeast Asia ~0.4 against ~0.2 (GCB 2025 Sect. 3.8.2). Regional shares are therefore not computed against a single total on this page.
